title: Stream Processing with Flink
description: Master event time vs processing time, watermarks for out-of-order events, exactly-once state via Chandy-Lamport checkpointing, windowing strategies, and Flink's checkpoint mechanism.

segments.text: Batch processing answers questions about the past. Stream processing answers questions about right now. When a fraudulent transaction happens, you need to detect it in milliseconds, not after tonight's batch job. Flink processes events with millisecond latency while maintaining exactly-once state guarantees — something Spark Streaming originally couldn't do.

Event time is when the event actually happened. Processing time is when the system processes it. A mobile user on a subway generates events at 3:00 PM, but they arrive at your server at 3:05 PM when they regain connectivity. If you window by processing time, the event is in the wrong window. Event time, embedded in the event itself, puts it in the correct window.

Watermarks tell Flink how far behind the latest event time to expect late data. A watermark of event time minus five seconds means: all events with timestamps before this watermark have likely arrived. When the watermark passes a window boundary, that window is considered complete and results are emitted. Choosing the watermark delay is a latency-completeness tradeoff.

Flink achieves exactly-once state using the Chandy-Lamport algorithm for distributed snapshots. Checkpoint barriers flow through the data stream. When an operator receives barriers from all input channels, it snapshots its state. On failure, Flink restores the latest checkpoint and replays from the corresponding Kafka offset. State and offsets are consistent.

Your Flink job processes credit card transactions. A checkpoint takes thirty seconds during high throughput. If the job fails just before a checkpoint completes, you lose thirty seconds of processing and must replay those events. How do you minimize both checkpoint duration and replay cost?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you optimize Flink checkpoint duration and replay cost for a latency-sensitive fraud detection pipeline?

segments.text: Three windowing strategies. Tumbling windows: fixed-size, non-overlapping — count clicks per five minutes. Sliding windows: fixed-size, overlapping — average over ten minutes, updated every one minute. Session windows: gap-based — group events with less than thirty minutes of inactivity into a session. Each serves different analytical needs.

Flink state backends determine where operator state lives. MemoryStateBackend: fast but limited by JVM heap — use for development. FsStateBackend: state in memory, checkpoints to filesystem — use for moderate state. RocksDBStateBackend: state in RocksDB on local disk, supports terabytes of state — use for production with large state. Uber uses RocksDB backend for their Flink jobs.

Late data arrives after the watermark has passed the window boundary. Options: drop it — simple but lossy. Allow late data with a configurable lateness — Flink fires the window again with updated results. Side output late events to a separate stream for batch reprocessing. Netflix allows five minutes of lateness for real-time dashboards with side-output correction.

When a downstream operator can't keep up, Flink applies backpressure — slowing upstream operators instead of buffering unboundedly. This is TCP flow control applied to data processing. Monitor backpressure in the Flink UI — sustained backpressure indicates a bottleneck that needs more parallelism or operator optimization.

Design a Flink pipeline for real-time clickstream analytics: count page views per URL per minute, detect session boundaries, and identify trending pages — all with exactly-once guarantees and five-second watermark delay.
segments.thought_prompt: Design a Flink clickstream pipeline: per-URL counts, sessions, trending detection, exactly-once.

segments.text: Flink provides true stream processing with event-time semantics, watermarks for out-of-order data, exactly-once state via Chandy-Lamport checkpointing, and flexible windowing. The key decisions: watermark delay balances latency vs completeness, state backend choice depends on state size, and late data handling depends on your accuracy requirements.
